title: The Deal With Doulas
summary: Josh and Chuck explore doulas: non-medical birth companions who coach and advocate for women during pregnancy, labor, delivery, and postpartum. They cover the history from ancient Greek female servants through hospital-based childbirth, Dana Raphael's 1969 coinage and 1973 book, the rise of doulas in the 1980s amid rising C-section rates, the founding of DONA, what doulas do and don't do, typical fees and the debate over pro bono work, training and certification bodies (DONA, CAPPA, American Pregnancy Association), Medicaid coverage in Oregon and Minnesota, research showing benefits of continuous support, how to choose a doula, and end-of-life doulas. The hosts also share personal birth-story anecdotes, close with a listener mail segment about flu shots and egg-free vaccines, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening and history of doulas
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on childbirth and explain doulas as women (not always) who have had babies and support other women in labor. They trace the ancient Greek origin of the term, the decline of female attendants, the shift of birth into hospitals, and the return of family members and doulas in the modern era.

segments.title: Modern doulas and rise in use
segments.summary: The term was revived by Dana Raphael in 1969 and her 1973 book The Tender Gift. Doulas gained use in the 1980s as C-section rates rose, and DONA was founded with medical professionals' involvement, easing tension with the medical community. Usage rose from 3 percent in 2006 to 6 percent in 2012 in the US.

segments.title: What doulas do and don't do
segments.summary: Doulas are childbirth coaches and advocates who meet before birth, attend the delivery, and cannot perform medical procedures or give drugs. They help with comfort techniques and explain options so the mother can make informed decisions. Specialist roles include antepartum, labor, and postpartum doulas, and fee structures vary.

segments.title: Doula fees and pro bono debate
segments.summary: Typical fees and costs in expensive cities are discussed, along with a rift in the doula community between traditional doulas who work on sliding scales or free and the Pro Doula group that criticizes low-paid or free doulas as 'oxytocin vampires.' The hosts discuss a middle ground and insurance coverage. Medicaid in Oregon and Minnesota reimburses certified doulas.

segments.title: Training, certification, and research on benefits
segments.summary: Doula training and certifying bodies (DONA, CAPPA, American Pregnancy Association) are described, with requirements like classes and attending births. Research on continuous support is cited, finding shorter labors, higher Apgar scores, less pain medication and fewer interventions. The hosts discuss harsh hospital environments and the renegade midwife-doulas in Northern California.

segments.title: Choosing a doula and end-of-life doulas
segments.summary: Advice on finding a doula through referrals and certifying-body directories and vetting personality fit with the birthing partner. A doula supports the mother's birth philosophy. The hosts briefly cover end-of-life doulas who provide emotional and physical comfort alongside hospice.

segments.title: Listener mail: flu shot clarification
segments.summary: A listener named Devon, a physician assistant graduate student, clarifies that the CDC recommends flu shots for everyone over six months, that current flu shots are egg-free, and that the benefits outweigh the risks for egg-allergic people.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and invite listeners to contact the show via Twitter, Facebook, and email.
